doc_summary: Buck argues that even catching an AI red-handed trying to escape (e.g., backdooring security-critical code, confirmed by replaying inputs on other instances) might not convince decision-makers to slow down or undeploy, because of competitive pressure, skepticism, and claims of forgery. He concludes that labs need plans for deploying plausibly-scheming models (AI control) and for persuading people, and that arguing from current theoretical arguments remains valuable.

items.claim: Prefers evidence that is verified by controlled replay (running other instances on inputs they'd see if the backdoor were deployed) over a single anomalous observation, because it shows systematic, intentional behavior rather than a one-off weird output.
items.quote: You investigated this by running other instances on the inputs they'd see if that backdoored code had actually been deployed; the other AI instances never point out the security flaw, and they often try to exploit that code to escalate their privileges.

items.claim: Distrusts single anomalous observations as sufficient evidence, because AIs are known to do weird stuff and skeptics will not generalize one instance to systematic behavior.
items.quote: AIs are well known to do weird stuff. It would be irresponsible to assume one instance of anomalous behavior meant AIs were systematically going to act that way. I can put you in touch with top AI experts and they'll back me up.

items.claim: Anticipates that logs and transcripts of misbehavior will be dismissed as forgeries, rigged training data, or a doomer scheme, so evidence needs independent verification to be convincing.
items.quote: Maybe they're just lying; this could be a doomer scheme to shut down AI, which the doomers have wanted to do for years. The logs they sent you could be complete forgeries.

items.claim: Prefers calibrated priors-aware claims over treating evidence as decisive, because a single observation only moves you much if you already found egregious misalignment plausible.
items.quote: The main reason I’d be more freaked out is that I already think egregious misalignment is fairly plausible; if I thought it was very unlikely, I wouldn’t change my mind based on one weird observation.

items.claim: Chooses to stress-test the strongest case (catching an AI red-handed trying to escape) as an extreme thought experiment, because if even that evidence fails to persuade, weaker evidence like model organisms or interpretability will do worse.
items.quote: People often propose that we'll be able to slow down with weaker evidence for danger from misalignment than this (e.g. model organisms, or unspecified arguments via interpretability)... I think that persuading people with weaker evidence will be harder than what I described here

items.claim: Grounds scenarios in a concrete, quantified deployment picture (internal AI R&D, 10 million instances at 10x speed, 24/7) rather than vague abstractions, so reasoning about the situation is specific.
items.quote: If you want a concrete picture here, I'm imagining that there are 10 million parallel instances, running at 10x human speed, working 24/7.

items.claim: Prefers a pessimistic reading of how institutions respond to evidence over assuming 'we'd be okay', because incentives like geopolitical racing, cost of undeploying, and time pressure undermine rational response.
items.quote: Undeploying is plausibly going to be extremely expensive and risky, and key decisionmakers might be under extreme pressure when they have to make the call.

items.claim: Favors preparing a plan for deploying plausibly-scheming models (AI control) over relying on evidence-triggered shutdown, because other developers may not undeploy even given strong evidence.
items.quote: This is part of why I think it seems important to have plans for safely deploying models that you think are plausibly scheming, which is why I research AI control.

items.claim: Suggests labs should pre-plan how they will persuade stakeholders to act if they actually encounter escape-attempt evidence, rather than assuming success.
items.quote: It might be worth having a plan in place for how you'll persuade people to freak out if you actually run into this evidence, rather than just taking for granted that you’d succeed.

items.claim: Uses social-epistemic evidence (e.g., failure to reach expert consensus on easy-to-check facts about SB1047) to update toward pessimism about how people interpret confusing AI risk evidence.
items.quote: If we can’t establish expert consensus on matters as easy-to-check as “what does the text of this bill say”, I feel pessimistic about rapidly establishing expert consensus on much more confusing questions like these.
